judge.reasoning:
The single most damaging flaw is a fundamental geographic mismatch with the brief. The owner explicitly restricted the search to "dense urban neighborhoods in the Los Angeles or San Diego metros" and to sites "near gyms, yoga studios, and office districts." Yet the report's entire thesis (title, summary narrative, Sections 1, 4, and the Tier 1 recommendations in Section 5) pivots to the Bay Area — San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Mountain View, Fremont, Dublin. None of these are in the requested metros. Section 1 is essentially an out-of-scope essay on "The Bay Area Affluence Corridor," and Tier 1 site recommendations are all Bay Area/South Bay. This is a critical failure to honor the brief and heavily discounts overall_quality and section_relevance. The best in-scope content (LA ZIPs 90034/90026/90066/90042, San Diego 92126, Costa Mesa 92627) is present but repeatedly deprioritized behind Bay Area markets.

Tool/metric selection is mixed. Good, relevant picks: age distribution (20s/30s cohort), labor force participation as a lunch-daypart proxy, and $150k+ household share. But the agent leans on uninsured rate as a "health-conscious" proxy (Section 1) — this is a weak, arguably spurious signal for a vegan-restaurant customer; it measures benefits/insurance access, not dietary or wellness orientation. Meanwhile genuinely decisive metrics for THIS concept are missing: population/daytime worker density (critical for "dense urban" + "lunchtime foot traffic"), commercial rent proxies to check the $7–10k lease budget, education attainment (a far better plant-based propensity signal than uninsured rate), and any proximity signal for gyms/yoga/office districts. home_ownership_rate is null. So tool_selection is only mediocre.

Narrative quality is fluent and internally consistent, and it does tie metrics to business logic, but it is undermined by the scope drift and by over-reliance on affluence for a $14–18 mid-range concept — ultra-wealthy suburbs like San Carlos/Menlo Park/Manhattan Beach are treated as prime when a mid-range fast-casual actually wants dense young-professional traffic, not the highest median incomes. Some claims also overstate (labeling uninsured rate a health-attentiveness proxy).

Data plausibility is reasonably good: county median incomes (SF ~$144k, Santa Clara ~$155k, LA ~$87k, SD ~$98k), labor participation, uninsured rates, and ZIP-level figures are within believable ACS ranges. Minor concern: some ZIP populations (~57k–76k) sit at the high end for single ZIPs but are not absurd, and 95051 showing 62% of households at $150k+ is aggressive but plausible for Silicon Valley.

Visualizations are well matched: bubble charts for multi-dimensional income/participation/age/population tradeoffs, bar charts for categorical city income comparisons, and histogram/violin for distributions. Chart types fit their data; this is the strongest dimension. Overall the report is competent analytically but fails the core mandate by recommending the wrong metros.
